questions.q: What is the Databricks CLI, at its core?
options: A command-line tool that wraps the same underlying REST API the UI itself uses
A completely separate system unrelated to the Databricks REST API
A tool only usable inside a notebook cell
A replacement for the Databricks Runtime
questions.explain: Every action covered in this chapter has a corresponding REST API call underneath it.

questions.q: What is a personal access token used for?
options: A long-lived credential that identifies you to the API in place of typing a password
A one-time code required only for creating a workspace
A setting that enables Photon acceleration
A Unity Catalog permission grant
questions.explain: It should be treated like any other credential — never committed to source control.

questions.q: How does `databricks fs ls dbfs:/FileStore/` relate to Lesson 8?
options: It mirrors %fs/dbutils.fs almost exactly — the same file operations, invoked from a terminal instead of a notebook cell
It has no relationship to DBFS at all
It only works if Unity Catalog is disabled
It replaces the need for a cluster to be running
questions.explain: Same idea, same operations, different interface.

questions.q: Why does real automation, like a CI/CD pipeline, need the CLI or REST API rather than the UI alone?
options: Clicking through a UI doesn't scale — automation needs something callable by a script, not something requiring a human to click
The UI cannot perform any of the same actions as the CLI
The REST API is only usable by Databricks employees
There's no real difference; the UI is equally automatable
questions.explain: This is the same underlying layer Chapter 5's Lakeflow tooling and external orchestrators ultimately call too.

options: Triggers a specific scheduled job on demand, outside its normal schedule
Permanently deletes a job
Creates a brand-new job cluster with no associated task
Lists every job in the workspace
questions.explain: Useful for testing a job without waiting for its actual scheduled time.
